prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, which brought optical frequency standards to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B053 for Katori and Ye as a single-part prize. The round-1 exchange sharpened why. The chair's central question is whether a lattice clock is a discovery or invention in the statutory sense despite the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlled single ions. I think it is, and the citation can say what is new without touching ion-clock territory: the magic-wavelength condition lets many neutral atoms be held tightly and interrogated at once without a light-shift penalty, and that is what carried optical standards to about 1e-18, roughly two orders of magnitude below caesium. The comb measures the optical frequency and the ion clocks control one absorber; neither contains the lattice idea. The result is reproduced at that level in several independent laboratories, so it is mature, and the two-name credit maps onto the achievement better than any competing configuration on the list. I would keep the case on fundamental-physics reach, meaning millimetre-scale gravitational redshift and bounds on drifting constants, and not on the redefinition of the second, which is a metrological milestone. As a circuit-QED theorist I have no stake in clocks, so I do not think field bias is pushing me here.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains that a precision-measurement invention built on two recently honoured enabling advances is of lower standing than a new window on nature (B009) or a closed fundamental question (B046), and that the prize should not drift toward metrology because it is clean. I have weighed that and still prefer B053, but the objection is not empty. A second weakness is that two names leave out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others whose work was real; the citation must be written around the lattice clock as a whole, as Kroll says, so neither Katori's proposal nor Ye's accuracy and many-body programme is subordinated. I have also noticed that my own preference is shared by the four members who hold it for reasons close to mine, and I do not count that as evidence beyond the scientific argument.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B046 first, says the Higgs question is closed while the clock is a refinement of an existing capability, concedes that three of four of Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee and Della Negra is arbitrary, and says he would not resist B053 if that allocation cannot be made defensible.
responses.response: I accept the scientific argument in full and have moved B046 into my alternatives in place of B001 because of it. We still disagree on what the clock is. I do not see it as a refinement of an existing capability: the lattice scheme made a different regime of measurement possible, and a two-order improvement over the primary standard is not incremental. My difficulty with B046 is the one he names. Any three of the four names is a choice among leaders of two collaborations of thousands, and a citation that honours roles rather than a discrete invention is hard to defend, particularly when the committee has not verified who held which role in 2012. I note his willingness to accept B053 if the allocation cannot be settled, and I think that is the honest position. I hold B046 as a strong second, not a first.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B013 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, argues that the 2016 prize did not cover the quantum spin Hall prediction, the Z2 classification or the HgTe observation, and rates the lattice-clock overlap with earlier prizes as closer than the 2016 overlap with B013.
responses.response: I take his overlap argument seriously and I have no good answer to it for B013: the 2016 prize was for topological phase transitions and not for the spin Hall prediction, and I do not count that overlap as disqualifying. The reason I do not prefer B013 is the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposal, which is the step that made the HgTe experiment possible and which a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp trio leaves out. A citation that does not name them has to be written very carefully around the Kane-Mele Z2 classification and the Molenkamp observation, and I would want the committee to see that draft before voting. On his claim that the lattice-clock overlap is closer than the 2016 one, I disagree: the 2005 prize gave a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize gave control of a single ion, and the lattice scheme gives many-atom interrogation, which is a different problem. I keep B013 as my first alternative and would move to it if the committee judged the omission tolerable.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B033, argues that the flat-band prediction and the correlated phases are stable and reproduced after eight years, and says he would be comfortable with B053 ordered ahead of B033 on timing.
responses.response: I accept his correction that the flat-band prediction and the existence of correlated phases at the predicted angle are reproduced widely, and that I should not call the whole field premature because the pairing mechanism is open. The prize would honour the prediction and the first observation, not the mechanism. My remaining objection is credit: Yuan Cao as first author of the decisive experiments, and others who established the field, cannot be named in a three-person limit, and an experimental credit that rests on a group leader invites exactly the dispute we are trying to avoid. I also note his own concession that B053 may be ordered first on timing, and I would count that as agreement on the order even where we differ on the merits. On B001 I am grateful for his remark that an adjacent circuits award so soon after 2025 is a poor use of the slot; I agree and my change below reflects it.

responses.point: Kroll prefers B053, says discovery versus invention is not a useful dividing line, argues the ion-clock overlap is separable, and asks that the citation be framed around the lattice clock as a whole so that neither Katori nor Ye is subordinated.
responses.response: I agree and I have adopted his framing in my citation. I would add one caution about his point on discovery versus invention. The statutes do allow an invention or improvement, but a committee that treats that as settled invites the objection from Pearce and Danielsson that it is giving the prize to a measurement tool; the better answer is to state in the citation what was newly made possible, namely many-atom interrogation at the magic wavelength and the resulting 1e-18 uncertainties, and to let the fundamental tests follow as consequences. I also take his remark about Ye's Fermi-degenerate many-body clocks and the comparison campaigns, and would not describe Ye only as the person who executed Katori's idea.

responses.point: Pearce moved B053 to first, but keeps B009 as his first alternative and says that if discovery in the strict sense outweighs invention, IceCube is the stronger candidate despite the allocation problem among Halzen, Karle and Spiering.
responses.response: His conditional is the right way to frame the choice, and I would answer it directly: if the committee decides that strict discovery must outweigh invention, B009 and B046 are the candidates to consider, and I would then ask whether they can be allocated. For B009 I cannot yet say that, since the diffuse flux is secure but the source associations at 3 to 5 sigma and the Halzen, Karle and Spiering split are both unsettled, and Pearce himself gave two different pairs and trios. I would sooner wait. I do not think the committee has agreed that discovery must outweigh invention, and the prize has honoured measurement achievements before.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a metrology advance as having standing equal to a discovery-type result such as B046 or B009, which is the question I cannot settle for others.

Whether a citation written around the lattice scheme can be drawn tightly enough to avoid overreach into ion-clock work and the comb, and whether the omission of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Hinkley will be seen as acceptable.
Whether the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang omission can be handled in a B013 citation, which is the one development that would make me move.
I rely on recollection for clock uncertainty figures, comparison campaigns and priority dates and have not verified them against the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. Circuit QED (B001) is my own research area (superconducting circuits, waveguide QED, microwave quantum optics), I lead the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, my Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson and frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum work in the field, and Chalmers hosted researchers associated with the 2025 prize. I should not be the deciding voice on B001, and I have removed it from my alternatives this round; I would also support the committee deciding how my view on B001 is handled, including setting it aside. I have no recorded connection to Katori, Ye or the other credited names for B053, B013 or B046, and no new connection has emerged from round 1.
